text:
Read-only audit task. Do not modify anything except writing scratch files under /tmp/saip_audit/.

Context: the dsh-chapters plugin archives DSH conversations into Markdown "chapters" (verbatim text rendered from the durable session log, with oversized tool results deferred to content-addressed `artifacts/` files). The project /home/adrian/Projects/saip is the first real project developed entirely through the `chapters` session preset. Its store is at /home/adrian/Projects/saip/.dsh-chapters/<sessionId>/{chapters,artifacts}. There are 8 session trees: three big ones (session-aac0254e-6da1-4f93-897c-c2336a97f829: 40 md; session-2edf9694-7635-4ef0-903e-d62cb435e8e6: 33 md; session-5b7481f4-89c2-4e22-b633-440dd9f7e2b0: 3 md) and five uuid-named subagent trees with exactly one chapter each.

YOUR TASK — evaluate the QUALITY and USEFULNESS of the archived knowledge, with numbers:
1. Structural stats across all SAIP chapter .md files: count, file sizes (min/median/max, total), tokens estimate field distribution from frontmatter (`tokens:`), `events:`, `artifacts:` counts, `unrenderedSeqs:` lengths, how many files have `subagent: true`, and the `generated:` provenance breakdown (how many title/summary/topics are `by: model` vs deterministic/fallback).
2. Title/summary quality: list every chapter title that is clearly a junk fallback or an artifact of the harness rather than a topic — e.g. titles derived from "Time sampled while preparing turn…", "continue", a bare agent id ("agent-acdab1f5-… sent"), or meta-titles about emptiness ("Empty conversation span with unknown events and zero-byte results"). Give counts and the file paths.
3. Verbatim fidelity / readability: pick 6 representative chapters (one from each of the three big trees + the plan documents + one subagent tree) and assess: does the body read as a coherent narrative of what happened? Are user turns, assistant turns, tool calls with arguments, and tool results present? Is reasoning captured (`_reasoning_` blocks) and is that useful or noise? Measure roughly what fraction of each sampled chapter body is: user text / assistant text / tool invocation lines / tool result stubs / omitted-host-injected markers.
4. Injection screen: count `⟦omitted:host-injected …⟧` markers across all SAIP chapters by kind (time-context, skills, AGENTS.md/instructions, runtime snapshot, TOC notice). Check whether any host-injected content leaked through verbatim into chapter bodies — search for tell-tale injected strings such as "Time sampled while preparing turn", "<system-reminder>", "workspace-write", "The following workspace instructions", "available_skills", "Current runtime context" appearing as real text rather than inside an omitted marker. Report each leak with file:line.
5. Artifact deferral health: for the 5 subagent trees and the big trees, count artifact files, total artifact bytes, and how many are the empty-string sha256 (e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855) i.e. zero-byte results. Check whether every artifact path referenced from a chapter body actually exists on disk (parse the markdown references `artifacts/<2hex>/<sha>.txt`), and report dangling references. Also report how many artifacts exist on disk that NO chapter references (orphans).
6. Are the chapters actually RETRIEVABLE knowledge? For 10 well-chosen queries about the SAIP project's own history (e.g. "why did we adopt Ink for the UI", "the four-platform bun single-file build", "the VRAM profile bug", "branch cleanup rule", "inference gateway plan"), test whether a plausible grep over the SAIP chapter text would find the answer, and whether the chapter summaries/titles would have pointed the reader there. Report hit/miss with the file that answers.
7. Redundancy: detect duplicated chapter content — same or overlapping `seqRange` values within one session tree, same title appearing twice, and near-duplicate bodies (compare sha256 fields and first 200 chars). Report the specific overlapping ranges/duplicates with file paths.
8. Plan documents: SAIP has `plan-001..plan-004` files in two trees plus chapter-like files whose titles are plan names. Assess the `kind: plan` documents: frontmatter shape, whether they duplicate a chapter's content, and whether a plan document is findable/consistent. Also check whether chapters contain a `## Plans in this chapter` block, and how many.

OUTPUT: a markdown report in your final message with concrete numbers and file paths, plus a ranked list of the quality problems you found (most damaging first). Mark speculation as hypothesis.Your parent agent id is "session-65fc8e2a-bd59-4bd7-ad3f-5a2bf9fa2a94". Before you finish, send your result to that agent with send_message({ agent_id: "session-65fc8e2a-bd59-4bd7-ad3f-5a2bf9fa2a94", message: "<self-contained result>" }). The parent shares your workspace but does not automatically receive your transcript, tool output, or reasoning. Send earlier messages as well when a finding changes what the parent should do next; sending a message does not end your turn.
